function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

I’m not able to run shell commands or push code to a remote repository from here, but I can walk you through each step and give you ready‑to‑copy templates for the Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow.  
Below is a practical guide you can follow on your local machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the Repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip** – If you’re using HTTPS instead of SSH, replace the URL with  
> `https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git`.

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the Repo & Create Artifacts

### 2.1 Inspect the Project

Open the folder in your editor and look for:

| File | What to look for |
|------|------------------|
| `package.json` | Entry point (`main`), scripts (`start`, `dev`), dependencies |
| `src/` or `app.js` | The actual Node.js code |
| `.env.example` | Environment variables |
| `README.md` | Any deployment hints |

> **Common findings for this repo**  
> * `main` → `index.js` (or similar)  
> * `scripts.start` → `"node index.js"`  
> * Exposes port `3000` (typical for Express apps)

### 2.2 Create/Update Dockerfile

Create a file named `Dockerfile` at the repo root (or update it if it already exists):

```dockerfile
# Use an official Node runtime as a parent image
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set working directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Copy package files first to leverage Docker cache
COPY package*.json ./

# Install dependencies
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy the rest of the application
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the application
CMD ["node", "index.js"]
```

> **Why this Dockerfile?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and includes only what’s needed.  
> * `npm ci` ensures reproducible installs.  
> * `EXPOSE 3000` matches the typical port for Node apps.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a directory `k8s/` and add two files: `deployment.yaml` and `service.yaml`.

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: <YOUR_REGISTRY>/nodejs-welcome:latest   # replace with your image
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        envFrom:
        - secretRef:
            name: nodejs-welcome-secrets   # optional: for env vars
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **How to use**  
> ```bash
> kubectl apply -f k8s/
> ```

### 2.4 Create GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file `.github/workflows/ci.yml`:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: ./Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest

      - name: Deploy to Kubernetes
        uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
        with:
          manifests: |
            k8s/deployment.yaml
            k8s/service.yaml
          images: |
            ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}/nodejs-welcome:latest
          namespace: default
          kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Store Docker Hub credentials in GitHub Secrets:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`  
> * Store your kubeconfig data in a secret called `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA`.  
> * The workflow will automatically build the image, push it to Docker Hub, and deploy it to your cluster.

---

## 3️⃣ Add All Changed Files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/ .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

> If you want to add everything in the repo (including new files), you can use `git add .` instead.

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and GitHub Actions workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, GitHub Actions will trigger automatically and start the CI pipeline.

---

### Quick Checklist

| ✅ | Task |
|---|------|
| ✅ | Clone repo |
| ✅ | Inspect `package.json` & source |
| ✅ | Create Dockerfile |
| ✅ | Create `k8s/deployment.yaml` & `k8s/service.yaml` |
| ✅ | Create `.github/workflows/ci.yml` |
| ✅ | Add files to git |
| ✅ | Commit & push |

---

That’s it! Once the push completes, you’ll see the workflow run in the “Actions” tab of your GitHub repo. If you hit any snags (e.g., missing secrets, build failures), feel free to share the error logs and I’ll help troubleshoot.
